```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

```{r load-packages}
library(tidyverse)
library(modelr)
library(broom)
```

## Task 1: Inspect the model matrix for cut

```{r task1}
data("diamonds", package = "ggplot2")

mm <- model.matrix(~ cut, data = diamonds |> slice_head(n = 10))
print(mm)

# Reference level: "Fair" (the first level of the ordered factor).
# The intercept column is all 1s.
# cutGood = 1 if the diamond is Good-cut, 0 otherwise.
# cutVery Good = 1 if Very Good-cut, 0 otherwise.
# cutPremium = 1 if Premium-cut, 0 otherwise.
# cutIdeal = 1 if Ideal-cut, 0 otherwise.
# A Fair-cut diamond has all four dummy columns = 0
# (its effect is captured by the intercept).
```

## Task 2: Fit cut-only model

```{r task2}
mod_cut <- lm(log(price) ~ cut, data = diamonds)

cat("Coefficients:\n")
print(round(coef(mod_cut), 4))

cat("\nExponentiated (price ratios relative to Fair):\n")
print(round(exp(coef(mod_cut)), 3))

# Interpretation:
# Intercept exp = $3,977: mean price of a Fair-cut diamond on the raw scale.
# cutIdeal exp ≈ 0.935: Ideal-cut diamonds cost about 6.5% LESS than Fair
# on average (raw data, not controlling for carat). This is the confounding
# effect — Ideal-cut stones are smaller on average.
```

## Task 3: Change the reference level

```{r task3}
diamonds2  <- diamonds |> mutate(cut = relevel(cut, ref = "Ideal"))
mod_cut2   <- lm(log(price) ~ cut, data = diamonds2)

cat("Coefficients with Ideal as reference:\n")
print(round(coef(mod_cut2), 4))

cat("\nR² — original ref (Fair):", round(summary(mod_cut)$r.squared,  5), "\n")
cat("R² — new ref (Ideal):     ", round(summary(mod_cut2)$r.squared, 5), "\n")

# R² is IDENTICAL. Changing the reference level is a pure re-parameterisation
# — it affects how the coefficients are expressed but not the model fit.
# The fitted values ŷ are exactly the same regardless of coding.
```

## Task 4: Add log(carat) to control for size

```{r task4}
mod_carat_cut <- lm(log(price) ~ log(carat) + cut, data = diamonds)

cat("Coefficients (controlling for carat):\n")
print(round(coef(mod_carat_cut), 4))
cat("\nExponentiated:\n")
print(round(exp(coef(mod_carat_cut)), 3))

# Now the cut coefficients are all positive relative to Fair, and they
# increase monotonically: Good > Fair, Very Good > Good, etc.
# cutIdeal ≈ +0.40 → Ideal diamonds cost ~49% more than Fair diamonds
# OF THE SAME CARAT WEIGHT.

# Why the sign change? In Task 2, we did NOT control for carat.
# Fair-cut diamonds happen to be heavier (more carat) on average,
# so their raw price is high — making Ideal look cheaper in a naive comparison.
# Once we hold carat constant (controlling for it in the regression),
# the genuine quality premium of Ideal cut becomes visible.
# This is Simpson's Paradox / confounding in action.
```
